articles.title: President Donald Trump Claims, "Tariffs Are Making Us Much Richer," but Economists Show They Have Unintended Consequences
articles.summary: The costs of tariffs to consumers, the U.S. economy, and the stock market may be considerably greater than the revenue they bring in over the next decade.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has been in the White House for nearly six years, spanning two nonconsecutive terms. Over that time, the iconic Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES:^DJI), benchmark S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC), and growth-dependent Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) have delivered well-above-average annual returns, compared to most other presidents since the late 1890s.

One of the key catalysts powering Wall Street's bull market, the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out, was well underway before Trump's second term began. But make no mistake about it: Wall Street and investors have also benefited immensely from the president's Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (signed into law in December 2017), which lowered the peak marginal corporate income tax rate to 21% (the lowest rate since 1939), fueling record S&P 500 share buybacks.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

President Trump's tariff and trade policy may be doing more harm than good. Image source: Official White House Photo by Molly Riley.

Tariffs are my favorite word. They're going to make America rich. It's making us much richer than we ever thought. We're taking in trillions of dollars.

While the projection for tariff revenue has, indeed, soared over the next decade, Trump's tariffs also come with an assortment of unintended consequences, according to economists.

President Trump is leaning heavily on tariffs

Although we've been hearing a lot about tariffs during Trump's second term, they've been a theme throughout his presidency. In 2018, the president imposed tariffs on an assortment of goods from China, sparking a trade war.

In early April 2025, Donald Trump unveiled his "Liberation Day" tariffs, consisting of a sweeping global duty and higher reciprocal tariffs on dozens of countries deemed to have unfavorable trade imbalances with America. These tariffs remained in place until the U.S. Supreme Court struck them down in a February 2026 ruling.

The president's newest round of tariffs was announced in late July, featuring a 10% to 12.5% sweeping duty on most imports from over 80 countries.

The purpose of these tariffs is threefold:

To encourage overseas companies to manufacture goods bound for the U.S. in this country

To make U.S.-made products more price-competitive with those imported

articles.title: Jamie Dimon warns US savers about Washington’s ‘heroin’ effect — it could crush you. Here’s how his bank protects itself
articles.summary: Hint: It prepares for trouble before trouble arrives.
articles.body:
Moneywise and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue through links in the content below.

Washington has a way of making the economy feel good. But Jamie Dimon wants Americans to look at what's fueling the high.

Speaking at the Economic Club of Chicago earlier this month, the CEO of JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM) compared government spending to a powerful drug — one that can boost corporate profits while setting the stage for a painful aftermath.

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

Gold has overtaken U.S. Treasuries as central banks' top reserve asset. Get Goldco's 2026 Precious Metals IRA Playbook for free

"We've got to remember about government spending: It's inflationary," he said (1). "It also does something which is unbelievable — makes you all feel good. It's like heroin. It drives your corporate profits."

For Americans watching their savings, that's a troubling combination. Businesses can report stronger earnings while the dollars you've worked to put away buy less at the grocery store, gas station and checkout counter.

Dimon explained how the money moves through the economy: "When governments spend a trillion dollars, that goes into spending, that goes into all your businesses. Machine tools, burgers, pools, homes."

"And then we all feel good because we're all making a lot of money," he said. "And it's a little bit of a false thing if it's inflationary, which it is."

Washington's borrowing habit gives that warning plenty of weight.

According to Treasury Department data (2), the U.S. government spent $7.40 trillion in fiscal 2026 while collecting $5.40 trillion in revenue, resulting in a deficit of $1.99 trillion — an increase of $217 billion from fiscal 2025.

Dimon made clear that his concern stretches beyond one administration's signature legislation.

"It wasn't the One Big Beautiful Bill, guys," he said. "We have been profligate now for years."

So how does America's biggest bank protect itself?

It prepares for trouble before trouble arrives.

"We prepare for low rates, high rates, stock price down 40%, credit spreads going up, bond rates at 8%, high yield at 15%," Dimon said. "And JPMorgan can handle all of that."

For everyday Americans, the inflationary pain Dimon warned about is already hitting home. U.S. consumer prices have climbed 29.8% (3) since the beginning of 2020, with energy prices soaring 53.5% (4) over the same period.

articles.title: Identity thieves don’t need your password anymore. Here are 6 new account takeover threats
articles.summary: Account takeover threats go beyond stolen passwords as criminals exploit session cookies, SIM swaps and MFA fatigue to bypass your login security.
articles.body: You may think of a stolen password as the main way someone gets into your account. But online criminals have learned that they do not always need to steal the password itself. They may hijack an active login session, convince you to approve a sign-in, take control of your phone number or use malware to collect information from your device. Passwords are still important. However, they are only one part of the security system protecting your identity. Here are six ways criminals may try to get around traditional password protection and the practical steps you can take to protect yourself. Join our CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Join us today, Saturday, Oct. 31, at 11 a.m. ET / 8 a.m. PT. Register for free now at CyberGuyLive.com. Missed this morning’s live class? Register at CyberGuyLive.com to watch the replay. YOUR BANK MAY STOP TEXTING YOU SIX-DIGIT CODES 1. Stolen login sessions When you sign in to a website, the service often creates a session that tells it you have already proved who you are. Your browser or app may keep that session active so you do not have to enter your password every few minutes. Criminals can sometimes steal the digital tokens or cookies associated with these sessions. If the service accepts the stolen information, an attacker may gain access without entering your password or completing another verification step. How to protect yourself: Review the devices and active sessions connected to your accounts. Sign out of anything you don't recognize and check for suspicious login activity. We've previously explained how to check for unfamiliar devices and remove them from your Apple, Google and Microsoft accounts. If you suspect unauthorized access, change your password using a trusted device and revoke other sessions when the service allows it. Remember that removing a device from an account list does not always terminate an active login session. 2. SIM swaps and phone account fraud Your phone number is often connected to email, banking, payment and social media accounts. Criminals may try to convince a mobile carrier to transfer your number to a SIM card or eSIM they control. If the transfer succeeds, they may receive calls and text messages intended for you, including certain account verification codes. A sudden loss of cellular service can be an early warning sign, especially when there is no known local outage. Other signs include an unexpected carrier notification about a device change or a password-reset message you did not request. How to protect yourself: Ask your carrier about an account security PIN, number transfer lock and port-out protection. These protections vary by carrier. For sensitive accounts, use a passkey, security key or authenticator app when available. Unlike text verification codes, authenticator app codes generally do not depend on your phone number. If text messages are your only available second authentication method, keep them enabled. They still provide more protection than relying on a password alone. ARE BANK TEXT CODES ENOUGH TO PROTECT YOU? 3. Fake login approvals and MFA fatigue Multifactor authentication, or MFA, adds another layer of protection to your accounts. However, criminals sometimes target the person receiving the security request. One tactic is MFA fatigue, also called push bombing. An attacker who can trigger authentication requests repeatedly sends approval notifications, hoping you eventually tap "Approve" to make them stop. Criminals may also impersonate technical support or a financial institution and ask you to read aloud a one-time security code. How to protect yourself: Never approve a login you did not initiate or share a verification code with someone who unexpectedly contacts you. If repeated prompts appear, deny them and check the account through its official website or app. Change your password if you suspect it has been compromised. When available, choose phishing-resistant authentication, such as a passkey or security key. App-based approvals that require number matching can also offer additional protection against accidental approvals. 4. Malware and risky browser extensions An infostealer is malicious software designed to collect information from a device. Depending on its capabilities, it may steal browser-stored passwords, session cookies, payment information or other sensitive data. These programs can arrive through fake software updates, pirated applications, suspicious email attachments, malicious advertisements or compromised browser extensions. Some malware operates quietly, which means you may not immediately notice anything unusual. How to protect yourself: Keep your operating system, browser and security software updated. Avoid downloading software from unfamiliar websites and review browser extensions regularly. If you suspect malware has compromised a device, use a separate, trusted device to secure important accounts. Run a security scan with strong antivirus software and remove suspicious software. For a serious infection, professional assistance or reinstalling the operating system may be necessary. Avoid signing back into sensitive accounts until you are confident the device is secure. 5. Malicious apps with access to your accounts Some criminals do not need to steal your password or infect your device. Instead, they may trick you into giving a connected application permission to access your information. For example, a fake productivity tool might ask to read your email, access your contacts or manage files in your cloud storage. You may encounter a legitimate-looking permission screen asking you to approve those requests. If you grant access to a malicious app, it may be able to retrieve information through the permissions you approved. In certain cases, that access can continue even after you change your account password. This technique is sometimes called OAuth consent phishing. In a September 2026 warning, the FBI explained that criminals can trick people into granting malicious applications access to their accounts. That access can remain active even after a password change unless the victim revokes the application's permissions. How to protect yourself: Review the third-party applications connected to your Google, Microsoft and other important accounts. Look closely at what each application can access. Remove permissions for apps you no longer use or do not recognize. Be especially careful with applications requesting access to email, contacts, cloud files or account management features. Passkeys can help, but they are not the whole answer Passkeys can significantly reduce the risk of traditional password phishing. They use cryptographic credentials associated with your device, security key or password manager. Unlike a password that you type into a website, a properly implemented passkey is tied to the legitimate website or service. That makes it much harder for a fake login page to steal the credential. However, passkeys do not eliminate every security risk. Criminals may still target an already authenticated session, an infected device, a malicious connected application or an account recovery process. How to protect yourself: Use passkeys when your important accounts support them. Protect your devices with a strong screen lock and keep recovery information current. If a service offers backup recovery codes, store them securely so you can regain access if your primary device is lost or damaged. Why changing your password may not be enough Changing a compromised password is important, but it may not automatically remove every form of unauthorized access. Some services revoke existing sessions after a password change, while others require you to sign out of devices separately. A criminal might also have established another route into your account, such as an app-specific password, an unauthorized connected application or a new recovery method. Your email deserves particular attention. Someone with access to your inbox could create forwarding rules that quietly send copies of your messages elsewhere. Review security settings for unfamiliar recovery addresses, connected devices, forwarding rules and app permissions. Remove anything you did not authorize. Also, check whether your password was reused elsewhere. If it was, replace those passwords with unique credentials. A password manager can make this easier without requiring you to memorize every login. What to do if someone gets around your password If you suspect an account takeover, act quickly. Start with the account that controls access to your other accounts, usually your primary email. Here's where to focus: A credit freeze is free and can help prevent criminals from opening new credit accounts in your name. You must contact all three major credit bureaus, Equifax, Experian and TransUnion, to freeze your reports at each bureau. If you believe someone has stolen your identity, visit IdentityTheft.gov for a personalized recovery plan from the Federal Trade Commission. The value of watching beyond the login Strong account security is essential, but identity misuse can happen outside the original account. A criminal might use exposed personal information to apply for credit, take over a mobile account or attempt financial fraud without triggering a traditional password alert. That's where an identity theft protection service can provide another layer of monitoring. These services can monitor certain financial accounts, credit activity and exposed personal information for signs of suspicious activity. Some also provide identity restoration specialists who can help you navigate the recovery process if your identity is stolen. Features vary by provider and plan, and no service can prevent every form of identity theft. For additional peace of mind, consider a service that offers monitoring, timely alerts and recovery assistance. See my picks for the best identity theft protection services at Cyberguy.com to compare your options and find the right coverage for your needs. Pro tip: Protect the accounts that unlock everything else Once a month, review active sessions for your main email and financial accounts. Remove devices you no longer use and check whether your recovery information or connected app permissions have changed. Pay attention to unexpected login alerts, changes to your mobile account and new financial activity. A short monthly security check can help you spot suspicious changes before they become a larger problem. FAKE CHROME UPDATE SCAM COULD INFECT YOUR COMPUTER Kurt's key takeaways For years, I've told people to use strong passwords and turn on two-factor authentication. I still stand by that advice. But what concerns me now is how criminals can get into accounts without ever knowing the password. Think about someone quietly reading your email through a connected app you forgot about or using a stolen login session to access information you've worked hard to protect. You might change your password and assume everything is fine, while that access remains open. That's why I recommend checking which devices and apps have access to your most important accounts. Start with email and your mobile carrier, because losing control of either can create problems with your financial accounts. And while identity theft monitoring services can help alert you to certain suspicious activity, they work best alongside strong account security. A few minutes reviewing your settings today could save you a great deal of trouble later. Have you ever received a login approval or password-reset request you didn't initiate, and did you take action or ignore it? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com Sign up for my FREE CyberGuy Newsletter CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Copyright 2026 CyberGuy.com. All rights reserved.

articles.title: Binance recovers 90 percent of stolen assets from hack
articles.summary: Cryptocurrency exchange Binance said Saturday that it was able to replenish 90 percent of the stolen assets ‌after a $6.3 billion hack of its platform. On Thursday, the money started moving out of Binance wallets, prompting the company to suspend all deposits and withdrawals. Some cryptocurrency firms froze around $3 billion in assets in connection…
articles.body:
Cryptocurrency exchange Binance said Saturday that it was able to replenish 90 percent of the stolen assets ‌after a $6.3 billion hack of its platform.

On Thursday, the money started moving out of Binance wallets, prompting the company to suspend all deposits and withdrawals. Some cryptocurrency firms froze around $3 billion in assets in connection with the incident.

“All BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD, and ZEC are fully backed 100%,” the company said in post on social platform X on Saturday. “We will continue to buy the remaining relevant token assets through market and OTC channels until the covered amount reaches 100% for all tokens.”

The company also said it will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not the users. In a previous update , Binance said it had set aside $6.34B in company funds to cover hacked losses.

President Trump said Friday that the administration is looking into the incident. When asked if the hack should be attributed to a suspected North Korean hacker group, the president said, “we don’t know.”

According to two blockchain intelligence firms, TRM Labs and Chainalysis, a North Korea-based cybercrime group TraderTraitor appeared to be behind the hacking incident. TRM Labs also noted that several aspects of the latest hack matched earlier North Korea-linked incidents like the $1.5 billion hack of crypto exchange Bybit last year.

In its Saturday update, Binance said after the 90 percent replenishment, the remaining 10 percent consists of “assets are less liquid, which means they may take longer to source in the required amounts.”

The company said the replenishment came from a partial deployment of the Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a portion of its Futures insurance fund and as well as Binance’s corporate treasury.

articles.title: 'Ferem diretamente o Código de Ética do Estudante de Medicina', diz CRM do Paraná sobre alunos que atacaram bolsistas e fizeram alusão ao nazismo | G1
articles.standfirst: Alunos denunciaram as ofensas ao Ministério Público Federal, que apura as mensagens enviadas após o resultado do 2º turno das eleições. UniCesumar afirmou que alunos envolvidos foram expulsos, suspensos ou advertidos "de acordo com a gravidade das condutas".
articles.summary: Alunos denunciaram as ofensas ao Ministério Público Federal, que apura as mensagens enviadas após o resultado do 2º turno das eleições.
articles.body:
Depois da divulgação de mensagens com ataques a bolsistas e referências ao nazismo em um grupo de alunos de uma turma de Medicina de uma faculdade particular de Maringá , no Norte do Paraná, o Conselho Regional de Medicina do Paraná (CRM-PR) informou que vai acompanhar o caso e "adotará todas as providências cabíveis".

Segundo o CRM, as atitudes dos estudantes ferem os princípios do Código de Ética do Estudante de Medicina, "segundo os quais o estudante deve estar a serviço da saúde do ser humano e da coletividade, exercendo suas atividades sem discriminação de qualquer natureza", diz a nota da instituição.

As mensagens foram enviadas depois do resultado das Eleições de 2026 , em que Lula foi reeleito presidente do Brasil .

Mensagens foram enviadas em um grupo com estudantes de medicina — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

A UniCesumar, instituição em que os alunos estudam, destacou que as trocas de mensagens não aconteceram nos canais oficiais da universidade e que adotou medidas disciplinares para punir os alunos envolvidos , incluindo expulsões, suspensões e advertências, "de acordo com a gravidade das condutas".

Alunos de Medicina foram expulsos e suspensos

Neste sábado (31), procurada pelo g1 , a UniCesumar informou que concluiu a sindicância que avaliou o caso e que adotou as medidas disciplinares. A reportagem questionou quantos estudantes receberam cada uma das punições, mas a universidade respondeu que não vai informar.

Em nota, a instituição de ensino também disse repudiar "veementemente qualquer forma de discriminação ou preconceito".

Alunos da instituição abriram uma denúncia no Ministério Público Federal (MPF) depois dos ataques. O órgão confirmou ter recebido a denúncia sobre as mensagens e disse que apura o caso.

Mensagens fazem ataques a bolsistas e alusão ao nazismo

As mensagens foram enviadas no domingo (25) em um grupo da turma. Em uma delas, um estudante sugere superioridade em relação aos bolsistas ao comparar quem paga a mensalidade com quem conquistou a vaga por seleção acadêmica de programas sociais.

"Quem paga trabalhou e tem 15 mil [reais] por mês para pagar >>>>>>> Quem passou numa provinha", escreveu um outro estudante.

Mensagens foram enviadas em um grupo com estudantes de medicina — Foto: Arquivo

Além disso, imagens e expressões associadas ao nazismo também foram compartilhadas nos grupos. Em uma das mensagens, um estudante compartilhou a foto do exército nazista acompanhada de referências ao "leite cru", expressão que se tornou comum entre grupos na internet que defendem a supremacia branca .

Print da conversa de cunho nazista. — Foto: Reprodução

Outra aluna criticou as ofensas e ressaltou que todos terão a mesma formação, independentemente da forma de ingresso. "Virou bonito ofender quem não tem dinheiro para pagar toda a mensalidade, como vocês? Todo mundo aqui vai sair com CRM [registro profissional para exercer a medicina]", disse.

O g1 optou por não identificar os alunos, uma vez que o caso ainda está sendo investigado pelos órgãos responsáveis e pode envolver menores de idade.

Ao g1, um estudante informou que tanto os universitários que fizeram as ofensas quanto aqueles que foram alvos das mensagens não frequentaram a instituição desde que o caso ganhou repercussão.

"É um clima hostil na faculdade, um clima hostil nos grupos, que vai muito além de divergências políticas. Parece que o contexto da eleição foi apenas um pretexto para eles extravasarem o ódio às pessoas mais pobres", disse o estudante, que preferiu não ser identificado.

Em nota, a UniCesumar afirmou que adotou medidas disciplinares contra os alunos envolvidos nas mensagens, mas não detalhou quantos estudantes foram atingidos pela decisão. Veja a íntegra:

"A UniCesumar comunica que concluiu no dia 30 de outubro a Sindicância Interna aberta para apuração dos fatos envolvendo mensagens trocadas em grupo de WhatsApp por alunos da Instituição.

A Comissão de Sindicância recomendou e a Reitoria da Unicesumar decidiu pela aplicação de medidas disciplinares em relação aos alunos envolvidos, nos termos do Regimento Interno da universidade.

As medidas disciplinares foram: desligamentos do quadro discente da Instituição, advertências e suspensões, de acordo com a gravidade de cada conduta apurada.

A UniCesumar reafirma seu compromisso com a ética, a responsabilidade, o respeito à vida e os valores que orientam a formação de seus estudantes. A Instituição repudia veementemente qualquer forma de discriminação ou preconceito.

O Núcleo de Apoio ao Estudante de Medicina (NAEME) permanece à disposição dos alunos para oferecer acolhimento, orientação e suporte, nos contatos (44) 99122-3957 ou (44) 3027-6360 ramal 2870.

O Conselho Regional de Medicina do Paraná (CRM-PR) informou que as atitudes descritas ferem os princípios do Código de Ética do Estudante de Medicina. Confira:

"Tais atitudes ferem diretamente os princípios fundamentais do Código de Ética do Estudante de Medicina, segundo os quais o estudante deve estar a serviço da saúde do ser humano e da coletividade, exercendo suas atividades sem discriminação de qualquer natureza.

A escolha pela Medicina exige compromissos humanísticos e humanitários, pautados pela promoção do bem-estar físico, mental e social dos indivíduos e da coletividade. Atitudes discriminatórias são incompatíveis com esses valores e não devem ser toleradas no ambiente de formação médica.

O CRM-PR adotará todas as providências cabíveis no âmbito de suas atribuições institucionais e acompanhará o desdobramento do caso, contribuindo para que haja uma apuração rigorosa e transparente dos fatos pelas instâncias competentes".

articles.title: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says that when Dario Amodei, Ilya Sutskever, Sam Altman, Greg Brockman and Elon Musk were all, I guess, one happy family, they were really ...
articles.summary: Satya Nadella has said that his views on AI have shifted in the past year.
articles.body: Satya Nadella has said that his views on AI have shifted in the past year. The Microsoft CEO was asked what he has changed his mind about in the last 12 months. His answer was about AI alignment, which is how to make sure AI systems do what people intend. Nadella started by looking back to the period around 2018 and 2019. He said that when Dario Amodei, Ilya Sutskever, Sam Altman, Greg Brockman and Elon Musk were, as he put it, “one happy family”, they were the real believers in scaling laws. Nadella said that was also what he believed in back then.What has changed Satya Nadella's mind in last 8 yearsNadella said the biggest change in his thinking is on alignment. He used to assume it would take care of itself.“When Dario and Ilya and Sam and Greg and Elon were all, I guess, one happy family, they were really the believers in scaling laws and that’s what I believed in back in 2018 and 2019. And I think the biggest change now I have is: ‘I used to always think that alignment will just fall out. I no longer believe that. So this alignment thing may be a harder, different problem. So that's the one thing I've changed my mind on,” Nadella said during an industry event in Germany recently.Alignment is the practice of designing AI systems so that their goals, behaviour and outputs match human intentions, values and ethical standards.Satya Nadella on companies, governments rushing to patch PHP flawsNadella also reacted to the crisis that unfolded after security firms recorded millions of automated exploitation attempts within hours of a PHP bug’s public disclosure. The uncovered vulnerabilities in PHP, which is the foundational programming language that powers a majority of the worldwide web, sent global corporations and government agencies scrambling to patch the critical flaw. PHP operates as an essential web-building block alongside fundamental standards like HTML and Python.“I’ve not seen anything like this in a long, long time. It was a long day and a long night, I know, for all the IT and security folks,” Nadella said, highlighting it is vital to build maintainable, secure software as architectures grow exponentially complex.From Tokyo to Helsinki, emergency shutdowns hit banking portals, rail services, flight bookings, tax departments and municipal communications – essentially triggering one of the most severe real-world stress tests ever faced by the aging, open-source codebases that keep people online, according to news agency Reuters.You use AI every day. articles.title: Why daylight saving time ended so early this year
articles.summary: Believe it or not, it’s time again for the twice-a-year clock change.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – They’ve gone and done it again. If you weren’t awake at 2 a.m. Sunday, you missed the clocks “falling back” an hour as daylight saving time came to an end.

Of course, you may have noticed when you woke up and found the clocks in your house that don’t match the time on your phone or laptop. Maybe it was how high in the sky the sun was when you awoke, or how early it seems to set on Sunday night.

You may even catch yourself pondering whether it really is the end of daylight saving time in 2026 already.

It is, but you also aren’t misguided in thinking it feels a little early for the clocks to be falling back.

Daylight saving time always ends on the first Sunday of the month, making November 1 the earliest date that we can set our clocks back an hour. That is what we’re experiencing this year.

Looking ahead, daylight saving time starts on the second Monday of March, meaning the soonest our clocks can “spring forward” is March 8. In 2027, that’s precisely when daylight saving time will start again.

It’s possible, through congressional action, that 2027 will be the last year that the U.S. changes its clocks.

Should the Senate pass the Sunshine Protection Act already passed by the House, and President Trump signs it into law, winters could feel different . Under the legislation, states that do not exempt themselves would observe daylight saving time year-round.

Generally speaking, that also means we would have later sunrises and sunsets than we have experienced between early November and early March. It’s the later sunrises in winter that didn’t sit well with some when the U.S. last observed permanent daylight saving time .

It’s difficult to say when, if ever, the Senate will pick up the Sunshine Protection Act. Many health experts disagree with the legislation , which could also impact how thousands practice their religion and your future flights , at least temporarily. The bill doesn’t have a “clear path forward,” either, according to Senate Majority Leader John Thune.

images.caption: A clock is seen during sunrise before the second round of the TOUR Championship, the final event of the FedExCup Playoffs, at East Lake Golf Club on September 22, 2017 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Ryan Young/PGA TOUR)

articles.title: Prop 45 in California could be hiding a loophole for data centers
articles.summary: Prop 45 would limit environmental reviews for “essential” infrastructure — one of the biggest controversies is over whether it would carve out loopholes for data centers.
articles.body: A high-stakes California ballot measure pitched as a fast track for “essential” infrastructure could wind up giving data center developers a loophole to evade public scrutiny, environmental advocates warn. Proposition 45 would shorten timelines for state-mandated environmental assessments for eligible projects and make it more difficult for residents to challenge those projects in court. Proponents say passing the measure would help alleviate the state’s housing shortage and meet rising electricity demand with new renewable energy projects. Environmental groups and some legal experts, however, warn that data center developers backing the proposition could escape scrutiny if Prop 45 becomes law. “The concern here is that data center developers will find a way to shoehorn their projects into the definition of an essential project and then get to take advantage of … the fast-track review that it’ll create,” says Fernando Gaytan, a senior attorney at the nonprofit environmental law organization Earthjustice, which opposes Prop 45. “Communities get cut out of the conversation.” Prop 45 would loosen standards for certain projects subject to the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). CEQA requires state agencies to perform environmental reviews and work with project developers to find ways to limit any harmful impacts to the environment and public health. Crucially, CEQA also mandates that state agencies gather community input and consider public comment before issuing any approvals. Specifically, Prop 45 would create a 365-day deadline for agencies to complete the environmental impact report for a project. It also stipulates that any legal challenges would need to be settled within 270 days. It would only allow for 45 days of public comment, and it would only require state agencies and developers to consult with Native American tribes that have been federally recognized. CEQA as it’s currently written sets a minimum rather than a maximum number of days for public review, and mandates consultation with tribes that might be impacted by a project even if they’re not formally recognized by the federal government as having “government-to-government” relations with the US. During the CEQA review process, state agencies develop alternatives that developers can take to mitigate environmental and health risks. Prop 45 would turn that on its head, making developers responsible for coming up with a single alternative project plan for regulators to consider. The proposition would also strip away an agency’s authority to repeatedly ask a developer for more information about a proposed project; state regulators would need to specify all the information a company is required to provide at the start of the application process. On top of all that, Prop 45 would bar courts from halting a project altogether even if it finds that the regulatory agency failed to correctly comply with CEQA. The judge would only have the ability to pause specific parts of a project that are problematic, rather than forcing a full stop to construction. That’s the piece that’s most egregious for Gaytan. “It’s hard to undo harms once you’ve already started a project,” he says. Data centers are a hot-button election issue for midterms across the US and have become a point of contention for Prop 45 as well. The proposition lists nine types of “essential” projects that would be eligible for streamlined review, including housing, clean energy, and “broadband Internet access.” Gaytan and some other legal experts contend that the latter designation — broadband internet access — could include data centers. The language includes any project that would “provide mass-market retail service by wire service, wireless service, or radio to customers in this state that provides the capability to transmit data to, and receive data from, all or substantially all internet endpoints, including, but not limited to, any capabilities that are incidental to and enable the operation of the communications service.” Proposed data centers that include any broadband transmission infrastructure might be able to squeeze into that definition, UC Davis School of Law professor emeritus Richard Frank and attorney Matthew McKerley write in a recent column in the Daily Journal. They also point out that companies currently developing data centers have poured hundreds of thousands of dollars into a campaign to support Prop 45. And while Prop 45 excludes certain types of projects, like nuclear energy and dial-up internet access service, it doesn’t explicitly bar data centers. Proponents, meanwhile, argue that Prop 45 would not apply to data centers. “The fact that data centers may play a role in supporting the Internet does not make them ‘essential broadband Internet access projects’ under Prop 45,” attorney and lobbyist Kurt Oneto writes in The National Law Review. The Yes on Prop 45 campaign didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Prop 45 has managed to garner support from the California and Hawaii chapter of the NAACP, which has been among one of the most vocal civil rights organizations to oppose data center developments across the US. The NAACP filed suit against xAI over air pollution from gas turbines at its Colossus 2 data center, and the Texas chapter has called for a statewide moratorium on data center development. “Working families and communities of color pay the highest price when essential projects like housing, clean energy, water, health care facilities, and transportation take years longer and cost millions more than they should,” Rick Callender, president of NAACP California/Hawaii State Conference, said in a September 9th press release. “Prop. 45 is about accountability, not shortcuts, creating a smarter process that gets these projects built sooner while protecting civil rights and environmental safeguards.” Regardless of whether Prop 45 influences data center development in California, its opponents worry that it could disempower the same communities that the new projects it covers are supposed to benefit. “It’s about public participation and democracy,” Gaytan says. “It’s about neighbors being able to say, ‘I want you to be transparent with me about what’s going behind that wall.’”
